steps.say: Everything is made of particles that are far too small to see. A particle is a tiny piece of a substance.
In a solid the particles are packed close together in a regular pattern. They cannot move around, but they vibrate on the spot.
In a liquid the particles are close together but not in a pattern. They slide past each other, so a liquid can be poured.
In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions. A gas spreads out to fill any container.
Particles never stop moving, even in a solid. Heating makes them move more.

check.prompt: Which state of matter has particles that are packed closely in a regular pattern?

options.why: Liquid particles are close but they are not in a pattern.

hints: Think about a state that keeps its own shape.
Particles in this state can only vibrate.
It is not a state that flows.
check.explanation: In a solid the particles are held in a regular pattern and can only vibrate.

check.prompt: Why can you pour water but not a block of ice?

options.text: Water particles are much smaller than ice particles.
options.why: The particles are the same. Only the way they are arranged is different.

options.text: Water particles can slide past each other but ice particles cannot.
Ice particles are not moving at all.

hints: Think about how the particles move in each state.
Pouring needs particles that can move past each other.
Ice is a solid, water is a liquid.
check.explanation: Liquid particles slide past each other, so a liquid flows. Solid particles are locked in place.
